quick: IV ~0.6 mg/kg (range 0.3-1.1 mg/kg) for intubation; titrate to effect under expert supervision
Not applicable - IV/IM use only under anesthesia and airway control
Used in obstetric anesthesia when needed; plasma cholinesterase is physiologically lower in pregnancy
Single intraoperative doses considered compatible; rapidly hydrolyzed
Use caution; avoid in pre-existing hyperkalemia
Severe liver disease lowers plasma cholinesterase - block may be prolonged
Not relevant to acute peri-procedural use
Neuromuscular monitoring, ECG, oxygenation, ventilation; core temperature for malignant hyperthermia
summary: Suxamethonium (succinylcholine) is the fastest-onset, shortest-acting depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, used to facilitate tracheal intubation and provide brief muscle relaxation. It carries a BOXED WARNING for cardiac arrest from hyperkalemic rhabdomyolysis in children with undiagnosed myopathy and is a potent trigger of malignant hyperthermia. It is hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase, so deficiency markedly prolongs paralysis.
indications: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate tracheal intubation
To provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation

dosage.n: Use a peripheral nerve stimulator; risk of Phase II block
Reserve pediatric use for emergency airway

dosage.d: IV ~1-2 mg/kg (infants need higher per-weight); IM up to 3-4 mg/kg
dosage.n: Per boxed warning, reserve for emergency/immediate airway need only

admin: For intravenous or intramuscular use ONLY, by clinicians skilled in airway management
Administer only with immediate facilities for intubation, oxygen, and positive-pressure ventilation
Do NOT give before unconsciousness is induced
Titrate to effect with neuromuscular monitoring; have atropine available for bradycardia
Store with cap and ferrule intact to avoid wrong-product selection (accidental use can be fatal)
moa: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Like acetylcholine it binds nicotinic cholinergic receptors of the motor end plate causing sustained depolarization (seen as fasciculations); because it is not rapidly hydrolyzed at the junction, the end plate cannot repolarize and neuromuscular transmission is blocked, producing rapid flaccid paralysis. It is then hydrolyzed by plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase, allowing rapid recovery.

absolute: Skeletal muscle myopathies (e.g., Duchenne muscular dystrophy)
After the acute phase of major burns, multiple trauma, extensive denervation, or upper motor neuron injury (severe hyperkalemia/cardiac arrest)
Known or suspected genetic susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia
relative: Plasma cholinesterase deficiency (atypical pseudocholinesterase) - prolonged paralysis
Penetrating eye injury or glaucoma (raises intraocular pressure)
Severe sepsis, prolonged immobilization, neuromuscular disease
Bradycardia-prone patients and repeat dosing in children

preg: Used in obstetric and general anesthesia when a neuromuscular blocker is required. It is poorly lipid-soluble and ionized, so placental transfer is minimal at usual doses; plasma cholinesterase activity is physiologically lower in pregnancy, which may modestly prolong effect.
lact: Single intraoperative doses are generally considered compatible with breastfeeding; succinylcholine is very rapidly hydrolyzed and unlikely to reach the infant in meaningful amounts.
renal: Use with caution; a single dose transiently raises serum potassium, so avoid in patients with significant pre-existing hyperkalemia (common in advanced renal failure). Routine dosing is usually acceptable in dialysis patients with normal potassium.
hepatic: Plasma cholinesterase is synthesized in the liver; severe hepatic disease (and malnutrition) can lower enzyme levels and prolong neuromuscular block.

major: Volatile anesthetics (sevoflurane, halothane) - increased malignant hyperthermia risk
Drugs/conditions causing hyperkalemia (additive cardiac arrest risk)
Plasma cholinesterase inhibitors (organophosphates, echothiophate, neostigmine, certain chemotherapy) - prolonged block
minor: Oral contraceptives may slightly lower plasma cholinesterase
interactions.diagnostics: Transiently increases serum potassium; raises creatine kinase and myoglobin with fasciculations

common: Increased intraocular, intragastric, and intracranial pressure
rare: Acute rhabdomyolysis with hyperkalemia in undiagnosed pediatric myopathy

monitoring: Core temperature and end-tidal CO2 (malignant hyperthermia)
Oxygenation and ventilation until spontaneous respiration fully returns
counsel: This medicine is given by an anesthesia provider during a procedure - you will be unconscious
Tell your anesthesiologist about any family history of high fever or problems during anesthesia (malignant hyperthermia)
Tell them about any history of prolonged paralysis after anesthesia (a cholinesterase enzyme problem)
Muscle aches for a day or two afterward are common
pk: Less than 1 minute after IV; 2-3 minutes after IM
Very short - hydrolyzed within minutes (plasma undetectable by ~2.5 min)
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; store with cap and ferrule intact
pearls: BOXED WARNING: cardiac arrest from hyperkalemic rhabdomyolysis in children with undiagnosed myopathy (e.g., Duchenne) - reserve pediatric use for emergency airway
A classic potent trigger of malignant hyperthermia - have dantrolene available
Prolonged paralysis with atypical/deficient plasma pseudocholinesterase - check personal/family history
Avoid in burns/crush/denervation injury after ~24-72 h due to upregulated extrajunctional receptors and lethal hyperkalemia
Pretreatment with a small defasciculating dose or atropine reduces myalgia/bradycardia
missed: Not applicable - suxamethonium is a single-use anesthetic agent administered by a clinician during a procedure, not a self-dosed medication.
overdose: Overdose produces neuromuscular block beyond what is needed: muscle weakness, reduced respiratory reserve, low tidal volume, or apnea. Primary treatment is maintaining a patent airway and full respiratory support until normal respiration returns. Prolonged or large doses may convert the depolarizing (Phase I) block into a Phase II block.
